subject: Nariway Signals - 2026-09-03 - Kennedy Center dismantles a sculpture without notice
html:
Nariway Signals September 3, 2026
 

Heaviest today on who gets to decide what stays on public view — the Kennedy Center dismantling a beloved outdoor sculpture without notice, a French court ordering a Gaza photograph reinstated after a town quietly pulled it, and the UK's own prime minister softening his call to send the Parthenon Marbles home — bracketed by a West Coast museum's financial collapse and one of the largest antiquities seizures in US history.

Lead

The Kennedy Center dismantled Joel Shapiro's “Blue” — and is handing it to the artist's own foundation

The 24-foot aluminum stick-figure sculpture — gifted to the Center and installed in 2019, since a genuine local landmark — came down September 2 with no advance notice and no stated reason, work the Center says was done “at its request.” A former curator has said he was told last September, under then-director Richard Grenell, to “get rid of” all the outdoor artworks because “the president wants all new art for the reopening.” The piece now passes to the Joel Shapiro and Ellen Phelan Foundation rather than into storage — a federal institution effectively deaccessioning a gift back to its maker's own estate-planning vehicle. Read against yesterday's lead, the State Department quietly weighing whether it can sell the Kehinde Wiley painting it pulled from its Santo Domingo embassy, it's the same pattern twice in two days: a government acting as a founder whose donor intent nobody can enforce.

Artnet · Forbes · Artforum

 

What's happening

A French court ordered a Gaza photograph back onto a wall a town quietly pulled it from

An administrative court in Caen faulted Deauville city hall for removing Jehad Alshrafi's AP photograph of a Palestinian football match from the Deauville Sport Images Festival in mid-August, ruling the town had shown no actual public-order risk to justify censoring an exhibition it didn't organize — the mirror image of the Kennedy Center story above: here a court, not a government, gets the last word on what a public exhibition may show.

ARTnews · PetaPixel

The UK's prime minister has quietly reversed himself on the Parthenon Marbles

As mayor of Manchester in 2023, Andy Burnham wrote “send them back, unconditionally”; as prime minister now, he tells the Financial Times it's “an issue for the British Museum, isn't it?” — as talks reportedly continue toward a long-term loan arrangement rather than outright return. A clean instance of how much a repatriation position can move once the person holding it actually has to answer for the institution.

The Art Newspaper

The Institute of Contemporary Art, San Diego is in financial and leadership crisis

The museum laid off almost half its staff — including its only curator — between late July and mid-August, has closed its main campus to the public, and faces calls for director Andrew Utt's removal after three years of mounted bills, bounced checks, and a 20% cut to its government funding. Former staff describe an institution that let “revenue generation” crowd out its actual mission — a smaller, blunter version of the stewardship failures this brief tracks at the billion-dollar end of the field.

The Art Newspaper

 

Worth reading

Anny Shaw, “The art world's billionaire problem is getting worse” — The Art Newspaper

New research finds roughly 150 works accounted for nearly 60% of global auction sales in H1 2026 — the clearest data point yet that the market's headline results now depend on an ever-smaller circle of ultra-wealthy buyers chasing museum-quality trophies, while the middle market stays flat. The demand-side mirror of every supply-side “boomer art dump” argument this brief has tracked since August.

The Art Newspaper

Roland-Philippe Kretzschmar, “The Trillion Dollar Wealth Transfer & How To Manage The Future of the Art Market” — The Art Bystander

Models what happens to auction houses, galleries, advisers, and museums under three different scenarios for how much of the coming wealth transfer actually reaches the market, and names valuation, documentation, insurance, lending, collection management, and succession planning as the businesses built to profit from exactly the moment Nariway's own clients are in.

The Art Bystander

 

To see — escalating

Christie's Alan Medaugh Hiroshige preview is now 8 days out

Inside two weeks. Public preview Sept 11–14, sale Sept 15, 20 Rockefeller Plaza; already on Alina's calendar for the Sept 12 preview.

ARTnews

The Bartos Mondrian's Zurich leg closes today; the free New York leg is now 14 days out

Paris opens in 6 days. Public-view legs: Zurich Sept 2–4, Paris Sept 9–12, New York Sept 17–20, Hong Kong Sept 25–29, London from Oct 8, sale Oct 14 (£20–30M / $27–41M estimate).

ARTnews

Sotheby's Open House is now 17 days out

Sept 20–21, Sotheby's NYC HQ. Its confirmed program includes a session on legal considerations across an art collection's lifecycle, staged by the house's own trusts-and-estates practice.

Sotheby's

 

For the record

US federal agents say they've seized more than 22,000 ancient artifacts in Florida

ICE Homeland Security Investigations' Tampa office, working with its Cultural Property, Art and Antiquities unit, recovered coins, ceramics, statues, and jewelry believed to originate from sites in Europe, Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean dating back up to 5,000 years, now under study with USF and Penn researchers — one of the largest antiquities operations in HSI history, and a scale reminder of how much unprovenanced material is still moving through the US for anyone valuing or insuring ancient and antique material as part of a broader collection.
